By KEN POWTAK
Updated 10:25 PM EDT, September 23, 2026
BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia’s Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians’ six-game winning streak.
It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday.
The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lead the AL in victories, joining Rick Porcello (2016), Josh Beckett (’07) and Curt Schilling (’04).
Gray allowed four singles, struck out three, walked one and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
Aroldis Chapman struck out the side in the ninth for his 35th save of the season.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) gave up a run on 10 hits with seven strikeouts.
The Guardians remained one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox atop the AL Central, after Chicago lost 5-4 to Kansas City on Wednesday night. The Guardians needed a win Wednesday combined with a loss by either Texas or Houston to clinch a postseason berth.
The victory came with a price for the Red Sox when center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela left with right hamstring tightness after running out a single the same day he was activated from the injured list. He had been sidelined with a right a quad strain since Sept. 3 and made a diving headlong grab on Steven Kwan, the game’s first batter.
Jarren Duran singled leading off the sixth, advanced on a groundout and barely beat left fielder Kwan’s throw with a headfirst slide on Monasterio’s hit.
Up next
Red Sox LHP Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) is slated to start the series finale Thursday. The Guardians had not named a starter.

Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA) finished his marvelous regular season with another strong performance, firing six shutout innings on 77 pitches, allowing four hits and one walk while striking out three. Next start? Game 1 or 2 of next week’s AL Wild Card Series, all but certain to be at Yankee Stadium.
“He looked fantastic,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “Had his spin. Was in the zone. Was ahead in the count. He looked really good. It was good to see.”
Even better to see was the return of All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman, who hadn’t pitched since Sept. 13 because of a lat issue. All the 38-year-old did was overpower the Guardians by striking out the side (all swinging) in order on 12 pitches. That’s all it took for career save No. 402 and 35th this season.
“I felt good and happy to be able to go out there,” said Chapman. “I felt like my pitches and my stuff were very good today. So I’m happy to be back. I feel normal. I feel like I’m at 100 percent right now.”
That is certainly good news for the Red Sox, who need their closer in top form to make a deep postseason run.
“He looked sharp,” said Tracy. “That was also really good to see.”
For the first time in weeks, Tracy was able to deploy his 7-8-9 relief crew in Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Chapman. All three relievers had injuries at various times down the stretch but are trending well now.
“That was great,” said Tracy. “To be perfectly honest with you, that was kind of planned out regardless of how the game went. So to be able to score a run prior to that section of relievers coming in was fantastic.”
And while hits with runners in scoring position (2-for-14, 11 left on base) were again a rare commodity for Boston, Andruw Monasterio broke out of an 0-for-21 slump by belting an RBI single with two outs in the sixth that scored Jarren Duran from second.
In a game in which neither team had an extra-base hit, combining instead for 17 singles, Monasterio’s knock was the difference in the ballgame.
“I was fighting myself just yesterday and tonight about my approach,” said Monasterio. “I just had to get through it. And I did it.”
In this final homestand of the regular season, the main focus for the Red Sox is having their house in order for what’s to come next week.
There was some cause for concern in that regard, as center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, after his first at-bat back from a three-week absence with a right quadriceps strain, had to exit in the top of the third with right hamstring tightness.
The Red Sox are hopeful it was a mild setback.
“I think it was just a cramp,” said Rafaela. “Maybe not hydrated enough. And I got that cramp right there and just didn't want to risk going for the double. And then, obviously, it’s Trace just trying to protect me, with big things in front of us. And so I think it's just that.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox pulled off a 1-0 series-evening win over the visiting Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night, despite the ongoing dearth of situational hitting that has plagued them for the last two weeks and intermittently throughout the season.
Boston batters tallied 12 hits, but went 2 for 14 with runners in scoring position, and left 11 men on base in eight innings.
Fortunately for the home team, Sonny Gray was on form in his final start of the regular season. The veteran right-hander tossed six shutout innings, with four hits, one walk and three strikeouts.
Gray’s sixth scoreless start of at least six innings this year tied his single-season high first set in 2015 and matched in 2025. He is the first Red Sox pitcher to make at least six such starts in his age-36 season or older since Luis Tiant in 1977, and only the fourth in franchise history (also Cy Young, Lefty Grove).
“Just a really good pitcher,” manager Chad Tracy said of his starter. “The level of consistency for him from start to finish has been very fun to watch, and impressive.”
Though Gray’s pitch count sat at 77 (52 for strikes) after the sixth and the game remained scoreless, Tracy went to his bullpen. With Boston’s postseason ticket punched on Sunday, the short hook could suggest Gray is getting the ball for Game 1 of the Wild Card series on Tuesday.
Cleveland southpaw Foster Griffin was not nearly as adept at keeping the Red Sox off the diamond. He struck out seven and issued no walks, but yielded 10 hits in six innings of one-run ball.
Save for Jarren Duran’s leadoff single and Andruw Monasterio’s two-out RBI single in the sixth, the Red Sox bailed Griffin out every time. They were 2 for 11 RISP through his six innings. Their nine men left on base during Griffin’s start included multiple in four of the first five frames and bases-loaded in the third.
“Yeah, I mean, take the positives,” Tracy said of the offense. “I thought we swung the bat great. We actually got some hits today. … Between (the two-out hits) and the accumulation of hits and base runners throughout the game, I thought it was a pretty good offensive night. Obviously you’d like to score more, but we did take better plate appearances.”
Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman, Boston’s elite bullpen trio all season long, ensured the slim lead held until the end with a scoreless inning apiece. Tracy revealed postgame their appearances were “planned out, regardless of how the game went.”
“That was great,” Tracy said. “To be able to score a run prior to that section of relievers coming in was fantastic.”
Duran, who replaced Ceddanne Rafaela in center field in the top of the third, led off the bottom of the eighth with a single. His subsequent steal of second made 2026 his second career season with 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases (also 2024). Duran, Mookie Betts and Jackie Jensen are the only players in franchise history with multiple 20-20 seasons.
Rafaela’s first game back from a 10-day stint on the injured list with a right quad strain began in energetic fashion. He recorded each of the first three outs, including a diving catch to rob Guardians hitter Steven Kwan of a leadoff single.
But after pulling up lame at first base on his own leadoff single in the bottom of the second, Rafaela ultimately left the game with right hamstring tightness when the inning turned over. Tracy announced postgame that Rafaela will undergo an MRI on Thursday.
“No, I think it’s more frustrating (than disappointing),” Tracy said of the Rafaela situation. “You want to see everybody get to that finish line healthy.
“So more just when you see it, you’re concerned, you know? So (we) don’t know where we’re at with it yet. Hopefully, it’s not a huge deal, but still, yeah, makes your heart jump a little bit, and we’ll see where he’s at.”
Cleveland threatened against Whitlock in an eighth inning that saw both teams run out of ABS challenges. No. 9 hitter Brayan Rocchio led off with a single, and Whitlock issued a one-out walk to third baseman José Ramírez before getting an inning-ending double play from designated hitter Chase DeLauter.
After the Red Sox stranded Duran in the bottom of the eighth, Chapman took the mound for the first time since Sept. 13. Boston’s All-Star closer was back in top form after being day-to-day with lat tightness. He struck out the side, Jo Adell, and pinch-hitters Angel Martínez and Angel Genao on 12 pitches.
The Red Sox are 85-73 with four games left to play. Wednesday marked Tracy’s first win since the interim tag was removed on Tuesday.

item.content:encoded:
The 30-year-old outfielder stole his 20th base of the season on Wednesday night, joining an exclusive club in team history.
BOSTON -- The Boston Red Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 1-0 on Wednesday night to improve to 85-73 and set up a rubber match on Thursday night. It was supposed to be a night off for struggling outfielder Jarren Duran; however, after center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela exited the game in the third inning with a right hamstring injury, the 30-year-old Duran was thrust into action, joining an exclusive list in the franchise's 125-year history in the process.
Duran's first at-bat in the third inning ended in disappointment as he struck out with the bases loaded to end the scoring chance for Boston. However, the 30-year-old turned in a strong performance in relief of the injured Rafaela, leading off the bottom of the sixth inning with a single, later coming around to score the game's lone run on a single off the bat of second baseman Andruw Monasterio.
Duran again reached base leading off the eighth inning with a sharply hit line drive to right field. With Boston leading 1-0, the speedster did everything he could to get the team in a position to add on. With third baseman Caleb Durbin at the plate, Duran took off for second base, diving in safely for his 20th stolen base of the year, securing the second 20-home-run, 20-steal season of his career.
Duran became just the third player in Red Sox history to post multiple 20/20 seasons, joining 2018 Most Valuable Player Mookie Betts, who did so three times during his six-year tenure in Boston, and Jackie Jensen, who accomplished the feat twice.
Reaching 20 home runs and 20 steals is an impressive accomplishment for Duran in an otherwise unimpressive season. The 30-year-old has been one of baseball's most disappointing players in 2026, hitting just .207/.265/.364/.629 in 147 games. The 30-year-old ranks in the bottom five among 133 qualified hitters in batting average (129th), on-base percentage (133rd), and OPS (131st).
Despite those struggles, Duran has still found a way to provide some value to the team in both the power and speed departments.
In other Red Sox news
Manager Chad Tracy told reporters, including Tim Healey of the Boston Globe, that Rafaela will undergo an MRI on his right hamstring. Rafaela described the injury as "cramping" that he felt on a swing, rather than when he ran to first base on his second-inning single.
As reported by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet is scheduled to throw another live bullpen session this weekend as he tries to return from left shoulder inflammation and join the Red Sox in a bullpen role for the postseason. Crochet will not make a regular-season appearance before potentially joining the active roster for the Wild Card round.
With a nor'easter expected to hit New England beginning Friday night, Major League Baseball has moved the Red Sox regular-season finale to Friday afternoon as part of a day-night doubleheader, starting at 1:05 p.m. ET. The league also moved up the start time for Friday's regularly scheduled game from 7:10 p.m. ET to 6:05 p.m. ET. As of now, no changes have been made to Saturday's game.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to win the series from the Guardians in Thursday night's rubber match at Fenway Park. Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) will make his final regular-season start for Boston, while Cleveland has not yet named its starter. First pitch is set for 6:45 p.m. ET.

Sonny Gray, Red Sox shut out Guardians, who remain 1 up on White Sox
(Photo credit: Gregory Fisher)
Andruw Monasterio's sixth-inning RBI single and Sonny Gray's six shutout innings propelled the Boston Red Sox to a 1-0 win over the visiting Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night.
The Red Sox (85-73) managed the lone run on 12 hits, all singles. They went 1-for-9 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base through five innings before Monasterio's run-scoring, two-out knock off Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) broke the deadlock.
In the sixth, Jarren Duran (2-for-3) lined a leadoff single to left and moved to second on a groundout. He scored from second base on Monasterio's knock, sliding ahead of left fielder Steven Kwan's relay throw and catcher Patrick Bailey's tag.
Gray (18-5) struck out three while allowing four hits and one walk to increase his American League-leading win total. Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman each threw a scoreless inning to finish off Boston's 17th shutout victory of the season.
Chapman struck out the side in the ninth to log his 35th save as Boston snapped a three-game losing streak.
Red Sox center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela returned from a 17-game injury absence caused by a right quad strain to record all three outs in the first, including a spectacular diving catch on Kwan, the leadoff hitter who still went 2-for-4 for Cleveland (82-76).
Griffin worked six frames, striking out seven and allowing one run on 10 hits and no walks.
The Guardians remained one game up on the White Sox (81-77) in the American League Central after Chicago lost 5-4 at Kansas City on Wednesday.
Rafaela hit a leadoff single in the second inning but appeared to be in pain after reaching first. He stayed in the game to run the bases and initially took his defensive position before Duran replaced him. The Red Sox announced that Rafaela was dealing with right hamstring tightness.
Rafaela's defense helped Gray retire the first six men he faced. Bailey recorded Cleveland's first hit with a leadoff single in the third, but a 6-3 double play ended the inning without any damage. Gray fanned a pair of Guardians to strand two to end the fourth.
After the lone run scored and Gray exited, Guerrero struck out three in the seventh after a leadoff walk. Whitlock worked around Brayan Rocchio's leadoff single and Jose Ramirez's one-out walk in the eighth, inducing an inning-ending double-play grounder from Chase DeLauter.
--Field Level Media

Jones’ place in the order is worth watching. Batting him third puts a right-handed hitter between Sogard and Abreu against a left-handed starter. It also gives Jones another opportunity to strengthen his case for a significant postseason role.
Offense Needs To Step Up
Rutschman gave Boston one of its few bright spots Tuesday, but the Red Sox could not build enough offense around him. Mickey Gasper’s pinch-hit homer tied the game in the eighth inning before Cleveland pulled out the win. Boston has dropped five of its last seven games.

Boston is postseason-bound. Wednesday offers a chance to start playing like it.

The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie year with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Adley Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs.

The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo.
Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a playoffs el pasado domingo, luego de que los Bravos de Atlanta ayudaran venciendo a los Astros de Houston.
Los Medias Rojas no pudieron celebrar con un triunfo en el bolsillo. Cayeron ante Tampa Bay en el último de la serie en Tropicana Field, pero eso poco importó, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta todo el camino recorrido para anotar su nombre en la fiesta de octubre luego de estar destinados al desastre en los primeros tres meses de zafra. Sencillamente nunca se rindieron, y eso lo reconoce Willson y se lo hace ver a sus compañeros.
«Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido»
«Primeramente, darle las gracias a Dios por todo lo vivido este año. Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido», dijo Willson a El Extrabase durante la celebración en el clubhouse visitante del Tropicana Field. «También hay que agradecer por el equipo que tenemos alrededor, los muchachos, la clase de personas que tenemos. Y de verdad que nunca dejamos de trabajar, ni de perseguir ese cupo a los playoffs».
En un buen tramo de la campaña, el primera base carabobeño comandó a la ofensiva patirroja. Primeramente, despuntó bateando por encima de .300 en abril y luego mantuvo la constancia suficiente como para terminar encabezando al equipo —con seis compromisos por disputar en el calendario regular— en cuadrangulares (27), carreras impulsadas (81), porcentaje de embasado (.387), slugging (.518) y OPS (.905).
Su escolta en el renglón de vuelacercas fue Wilyer Abreu (24), que no solo aportó con el bate, sino con su prodigiosa defensa en los jardines que lo tiene como firme candidato a obtener su tercer guante de oro consecutivo.
Elogios para Abreu y Monasterio
«Estoy orgulloso de todos mis compañeros, especialmente de Wilyer; por todo lo que ha hecho este año y lo que ha logrado, ha sido bastante importante, igual que (Andruw) Monasterio, que lo trajeron para acá a hacer un trabajo. Se amoldó muy bien a su rol y mira, esto es lo que hace un equipo unido, clasificar», añadió.
«Estoy verdaderamente orgulloso del equipo que formamos y que tenemos ahora mismo», acotó Wilyer, que comanda a los jardineros derechos de la Liga Americana en Carreras Salvadas a la Defensiva con 26. «Le dimos la vuelta a la temporada de una forma increíble. Me siento orgulloso de haber sido parte de esto, de poder ayudar y contribuir al equipo en este momento y durante toda la temporada».
Wilyer también destaca entre los jugadores de su posición en el nuevo circuito siendo segundo en Outs Por Encima del Promedio (3) y primero en valor en carreras de fildeo (5). Igualmente, despunta en asistencias desde los jardines (12) y en el apartado ofensivo, lidera a los Medias Rojas en carreras anotadas (81), dobles (36, con lo que comanda la Liga Americana) y bases por bolas (70). El zuliano estableció topes personales en las categorías ofensivas antes mencionadas, además de traídas al plato (74), imparables (144) y, por supuesto, bambinazos (24).
Monasterio ha entendido su rol
Por su parte, Andruw Monasterio supo adaptarse a su rol de pelotero de reemplazo, con tramos destacados a la ofensiva. Un ejemplo de ello fue julio. En ese entonces asumió la titularidad de las paradas cortas en ausencia del lesionado Trevor Story, lo que coincidió con la racha de 15 triunfos seguidos que le dio vida a Boston. Exhibió un promedio de .338 (de 65-22), OBP de .413, slugging de .631 y OPS de 1.044, con tres cuadrangulares, 11 producidas y nueve anotadas.
Pero no se limitó al campo corto; Monasterio también vio acción en segunda, en primera, e incluso en tercera.
«Para mí, todo fue amoldarme a mi rol», comentó Monasterio a El Extrabase. «Fui al Spring Training y me gané el puesto. Súper contento porque son cuatro años en el show y cuatro años clasificando, es una bendición. Es muy satisfactorio, porque tú trabajas mucho para esto, para este momento del año, el béisbol en octubre».
Suárez ha sido clave en el tramo final
En el renglón del pitcheo, Ranger Suárez ha sido clave en este tramo final de la zafra, luego de presentar altibajos durante gran parte del año e incluso estar en lista de lesionados después de la pausa del juego de estrellas.
En sus últimas cinco aperturas exhibe foja de 3-1 y una efectividad de 2.70 en 30 innings de labor, con 22 ponches, 12 pasaportes y un WHIP de 1.27. Todo eso ha confluido en una actuación general en su primera contienda en la Liga Americana, en la que posee un promedio de carreras limpias de 3.27 en 143.1 capítulos de trabajo a lo largo de 27 salidas.
«Contento del sacrificio que hicimos durante la temporada, especialmente por cómo empezamos», expresó el zurdo de Pie de Cuesta. «Entonces, mira lo que nos recompensó Dios, estamos en los playoffs».
A Ranger se lo ha caracterizado por ser un lanzador bastante calmado, casi imperturbable. Y bastante de eso mostró el equipo para lograr revertir su situación de inicio de temporada. «No comenzamos de la manera que queríamos, pero el talento de los muchachos es increíble. Sabíamos que le íbamos a dar vuelta a la situación».

item.content:encoded:
In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith.
Nearly halfway through the season, at the bottom of a bad American League, in a sport dominated by data and measurables, virtually all available evidence led to a consistent conclusion: The 2026 Red Sox were just not good. They fired the manager a month in. They lost key players to long-term injuries. They showed little life.
And so they were left with mere belief. Belief in themselves, belief that they could salvage it, belief that how could it possibly stay like this forever?
“We all still had faith in each other,” Garrett Whitlock said. “Human beings still do the thing. All the numbers and data would have counted us out and all that kind of stuff. And the players in this clubhouse were like, hey, we can stick with this.”
Or, at least, that’s what they said.
“We wouldn’t have said it if we didn’t believe it,” Caleb Durbin said.
Improbably, incredibly, here they are. They clinched a spot in the postseason Sunday, allowing aspirations of late October in a season that felt over in June.
The moments that marked their ascent were many, an almost endless series of sliding doors and what ifs, minor-turned-monumental plays. Recently, in a series of interviews, some of these Sox reflected on their favorites.
“The fun thing about a season,” Durbin said, “is that there’s a whole lot of moments you can look back on that tell the story.”
The Schlitt Show
The date: June 25
The playoff odds (via FanGraphs): 10.6 percent
The moment: Caleb Durbin homers off Cam Schlittler
Remember how dire it felt on June 25. In the end, it was the start of the Red Sox’ run.
When Boston had last played at Fenway Park, it got swept by the Blue Jays, including a gut-wrenching finale in which the Sox rallied for a late tie only to lose. Emanating from the stands were loud boos and chants of “sell the team,” sentiments and sounds burned into the players’ psyche.
Just before they returned, the Sox dramatically dropped two of three to the Rockies. Durbin partially dislocated his left pinkie finger sliding head-first into first base. On the way back from Colorado, plane problems delayed their Boston arrival to 5 a.m., about 14 hours before the first pitch of a four-game series against the Yankees.
“And,” Isiah Kiner-Falefa said, “Schlittler.”
On the mound that night was righthander Cam Schlittler, the Walpole native and emerging Yankees ace, who ended the Red Sox’ season last year.
The weekend was ripe for misery. And it was the beginning of everything.
“It’s a very discernible line in the sand: the Yankees series at home,” interim manager Chad Tracy said.
The Red Sox were hitting like they had barely slept the night before, so Schlittler cruised into the fifth inning. But when a Yankees fielding error prolonged the frame, the Sox managed to tie it. Up came Durbin with the go-ahead run on base.
Durbin, back in the lineup a day after popping that pinkie back into place, homered to left field — just high enough and just far enough, off the lip of the Green Monster.
The dirt dog Durbin? Against that team, off that pitcher, after that travel and those losses?
“That was the big defining moment of the year,” Kiner-Falefa said. “Turned the whole attitude of the team around.”
The Red Sox trailed for half of an inning the rest of the series, sweeping all four games.
Still in a huge hole, they were 10 games under .500 at 36-46. But for the first time, they had something tangible to build on, not just blind belief.
“Right there is when it changed,” Tracy said. “Oh my God, that was awesome. But like, was that a blip? That’s what people think.”
The comeback
The date: July 12
The playoff odds: 40.5 percent
The moment: Francisco Lindor’s error leads to ninth consecutive win
Against the Angels, against the White Sox, after an overnight flight delay trying to escape Chicago, despite rolling up to Citi Field just two hours before scheduled first pitch, the Red Sox won eight consecutive games to take them into mid-July.
It was a significant accomplishment, especially considering it took them three months to win more than three in a row.
Unfortunately for the Sox, that is where the win streak was going to end. The Red Sox had one hit heading into the ninth inning against the Mets.
With a runner on first base and one out in the ninth, Romy Gonzalez hit a hard ground ball right at Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor. It was a ready-made double play. The game was over, and so was the streak … until it wasn’t.
“The guy has a Platinum Glove,” Whitlock said.
“Oh, now it’s our turn,” Connor Wong said. “Everything was going wrong for us, and then the one thing kind of went right for us.”
“He makes that play, we lose. And we somehow win that game,” Durbin said. “That was probably our biggest game of the year. Not because of who we beat, but because of the way we won that game.”
Lindor failed to turn the double play. He failed to get even one out. The ball ricocheted off his chest, everybody was safe, Devin Williams lost the strike zone, Durbin walked to load the bases, Andruw Monasterio walked to force in a run, and Jarren Duran singled to bring in the tying run. The Red Sox won in 10 innings.
Opportunity knocked, and the Red Sox kicked the door down. It was the difference between an 8-1 road trip, a solid week-plus with a total dud of a loss heading into the break ... and a stunning 9-0, feeling great going into four days off, with a chance to bring the momentum home.
If the win streak had ended at eight, would the Sox have won the next six after the break? Would they have grabbed such a strong hold on a wild-card spot? Would they have known what it felt like to stage late comebacks — the theme of their summer surge?
“Even that ninth inning, though, we needed five people to do the job, and they all did. That was the first time that happened,” Durbin said. “That kind of sparked the feeling of OK, we’re a team that if we need to get something going, we can.”
Tracy said: “Two weeks ago, we were pretty entrenched as the worst team in the American League. Now, we were holding a spot or were really close. I felt like that was — for the whole group — all right, we have turned this around and we have a legitimate chance now.”
The homecoming
The date: July 17-22
The playoff odds: 50.3 percent to 61 percent
The moment: “There’s so many,” Tracy said, leading to six more wins
Upon returning from the All-Star break, the Red Sox reached the chaotic, fever dream, how-is-this-possible portion of their turnaround.
Every game — four more wins against the Rays, then two against the Orioles — seemed to bring out a more electric version of Fenway Park than the one before.
For the Red Sox, that was the most gratifying. Their lowest low, several players said, wasn’t getting dumped in Denver. It was struggling in Boston and hearing it from the home crowds. They went 17-27 at Fenway in the first half.
How to pick just one moment?
For win No. 10, the first game back from the break, the Red Sox beat Tampa Bay, 10-0. It was resounding.
“That was like an important statement game for us,” Greg Weissert said.
For No. 11, the second game of a doubleheader, the Rays scored two runs in the top of the first and the Red Sox came right back with three in the bottom half. That got them back to .500 and into a tie for a playoff spot.
“Relentlessness,” Trevor Story said.
For No. 12, Wilyer Abreu’s fourth homer in two games was a go-ahead shot off Garrett Cleavinger, capping a four-run rally in the seventh for the Sox’ first lead of the day.
“When you win that many games in a row, there’s usually three or four of them that you’re probably not supposed to win,” Tracy said.
For No. 13, Sonny Gray tossed a quality start in an actual low-stress afternoon.
“It’s hard to remember everything,” Wong said.
For No. 14, Durbin went deep again, in the eighth against Tyler Wells to break a tie. Fourth-string shortstop Tsung-Che Cheng recorded the final out with a leaping catch of a line drive to save two runs.
Even for the Red Sox, the believers, it strained belief.
“It comes off the bat and you’re like, ‘Oh no.’ And [Cheng] out of nowhere snares it,” Tracy said. “Everybody’s fired up in the coach’s room and you fist bump. You shake your head like: ‘Holy [expletive]. We did it again.’ There were plenty of those for sure behind the scenes.”
For No. 15, they scored four runs in the first inning, leaving no doubt and matching the franchise record win streak set in 1946.
Later that day, July 22, the Red Sox lost the second game of a doubleheader. The streak was over — for real this time. The season is not.
That 15-0 run was part of 27-3 and 32-5 stretches, some of the wildest in franchise history.
“It was maybe the beginning of August, I think, when someone was like, ‘Hey, you realize we’re six games up in the wild card, right?’” said Whitlock, not a standings tracker. “Wait, what?”
“That’s a testament to the people that we have,” Durbin said. “As a player, we have talent. We have a lot of talent to do the job. But [after] the start we had, it takes the person to continue to push forward and come out of it the way we did.”
“I never doubted it, our ability to come together at some point and turn this thing around,” interim bench coach José David Flores said. “To be honest with you, it was kind of shocking the way we did it.”

Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Red Sox mailbag: Should Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck be on playoff roster?
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store. But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag. Tanner Houck and Gar
item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

When the Boston Red Sox lost shortstop Trevor Story to an injury earlier this year, one big question was how they were going to replace him. Interim manager Chad Tracy used a couple of different players who more than held things down until the veteran was going to return.
When Story was eligible to return, Andruw Monasterio found himself as the odd man out at shortstop. However, Story had to prove that he was healthy enough to hold down the job late in the season.
As it turns out, he is. After coming up clutch on Thursday night, Story didn't mince words about the noise that there is outside the locker room about him.
Boston Red Sox Shortstop Trevor Story Drops Honest Quote on Outside Noise
Trailing 3-0 against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night in Arlington, Boston was staring at being swept as the game moved into the late innings. After they plated a run in the top of the seventh on a Roman Anthony fielder's choice.
In the top of the eighth, Story stepped up to the plate with two runners on and one out. Story crushed a curveball from Texas' Jacob Latz for a three-run home run and 4-3 lead. The Red Sox got the final six outs to secure a one-run win. After the game, Story didn't mince words about the outside noise and hearing it.
"I'm not really motivated by outside noise, but you hear it," said Story, per Alex Speier of the Boston Globe. "I try to use it in the way that fits me best. The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be, and it's starting to show."
Halfway through the month of September, Story is slashing .327/.339/.473 in September with one home run and six RBIs.
"He's been great," Tracy said, per Perla Paredes of MLB.com. "He's got a hit in every game but one. That was a hell of an at-bat against a really good pitcher in a really big spot and a huge swing. Obviously needed a win, but all the credit to him.
"You're one pitch away in a spot like that, where he can change a game, like we saw it numerous times in the second half of last year. So, like I said, it was a massive swing."
Trevor Story Looking To Find Swing Before Playoffs
There are nine games for the Red Sox before the playoffs begin. Boston is likely headed for an American League wild-card series against the New York Yankees. The series for the second straight year will be in the Bronx.
Boston has a three-game series against the first-place Tampa Bay Rays this weekend in Central Florida. They then close out the season with a pair of three-game series at home against the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs.
Finishing the regular season strong will be key. Boston has struggled in September and is limping into the playoffs. A healthy Story could be key for Boston come postseason baseball.

Boston Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin dislocated his left pinky in late June. He reinjured it early last month.
Before the Red Sox’s upcoming series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field, Durbin told the Boston Globe’s (subscription required) Alex Speier his pinky is still bothering him.
Boston Red Sox 3B Caleb Durbin Makes Statement on Injury Before Rays series
Durbin said his pinky doesn’t “quite straighten or bend all the way.”
The third baseman received X-Rays after he initially injured his pinky in June and after he reinjured it in August. Both times, the X-rays revealed there was no fracture.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” Durbin said.
Speier asked Durbin if he needs offseason surgery.
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
Read More: Pinkie injury may be affecting Caleb Durbin, but it’s not keeping him out of Red Sox lineup
Despite his pinky injury, Durbin hasn’t been placed on the injured list at all this season.
Looking at Boston Red Sox 3B Caleb Durbin
On Feb. 9, the Red Sox acquired Durbin, shortstop Andruw Monasterio, second baseman Anthony Seigler and future considerations from the Milwaukee Brewers for second baseman David Hamilton and left-handers Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan.
Durbin, 26, has hit .248/.333/.381 with 13 home runs and 64 RBI over 145 games with Boston this year.
Durbin made his MLB debut with the Brewers last season. He hit .256/.334/.387 with 11 home runs and 53 RBI during his rookie year.
The Red Sox will begin their series against the Rays at 7:10 p.m. EDT on Friday.

item.content:encoded:
We won't spend too long belaboring how bad the Kyle Harrison-Caleb Durbin looked for the Boston Red Sox after a few months; the southpaw had emerged as a genuine National League Cy Young contender for the Milwaukee Brewers in the first half, while the third baseman was one of the league's worst qualified hitters through the beginning of June. Tack on the fact that Shane Drohan has become a valuable starter in his own right this year while Andruw Monasterio has been worth negative fWAR, and you've got a recipe for an all-time disaster of a trade.
And yet, after the tide began shifting over the summer, we can now definitively say the pendulum has swung back in the other direction. Durbin has been a star since June 1, posting an .812 OPS and a 129 wRC+. Meanwhile, Harrison is struggling so badly that he's now been moved out of the Brewers' rotation entirely.
It's far too early to suggest that the Red Sox have made up that early gap and are now the winners of the blockbuster trade, but it's clear that their decision to go all-in for Durbin wasn't a foolish one.
Red Sox just need to break even now to win Caleb Durbin trade in the future
In that same post-June-1 span, Harrison has pitched to an 6.10 ERA and 5.38 FIP, allowing a whopping 17 home runs over just 59 innings. A bout with forearm tightness near the All-Star break definitely has something to do with his second-half collapse, but he hasn't been pitching like an ace for quite a while. The fact that there's been conversations about him being left off the Brewers' postseason roster entirely should tell you all you need to know about the southpaw's recent struggles.
Durbin is trending in the exact opposite direction, as he's currently the seventh-most valuable third baseman in the league by fWAR (2.9) this season. A lot of that has to do with how excellent his baserunning and glove have been, but saying that someone is above average in every phase of the game isn't exactly a bad thing. He's a couple of steals and some favorable votes away from a 20 SB, Gold Glove campaign in his Red Sox debut. Not too shabby, eh?
It's also worth factoring in the other players Craig Breslow pried out of Milwaukee; neither Monasterio nor Anthony Seigler have been great in limited duty in Boston, but the former has produced some timely hits while playing all four infield positions while the latter has a 102 wRC+ in just under 175 plate appearances this year.
Then there's Owen Hull, whom the Red Sox selected with the compensatory draft pick the Brewers forked over in the trade. All he did after being drafted was mash in High-A, posting a .967 OPS in 24 games.
With Durbin under contract through 2031 and Hull sure to fly up the prospect rankings over the offseason, there's a good chance that the Sox can win this trade down the road, so long as they continue to break even for now.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox recalled Anthony Seigler less than a week ago to help fill the roster gap left by Eli White's foot injury. The switch-hitting infielder had contributed during a stretch that lifted Boston into playoff contention.
That fill-in role has already been cut short. Seigler went on the injured list September 13 with a right wrist issue, and the latest update paints a discouraging picture for his availability going forward.
The Red Sox are 82-70 with 10 games left in the regular season. The playoff spot is within reach. The roster is getting thinner.
Infielder Shut Down From Baseball Activities
Seigler has been shut down from all baseball activities for at least a week, according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo.
The wrist flared up again during a plate appearance on Sunday, and he now appears doubtful to return during the regular season.
The timeline makes the math difficult. A minimum of seven days without baseball activities leaves almost no runway to ramp back up before the final game of the season. Even an optimistic recovery would push his return deep into October, if it comes at all.
What Seigler Brought to Boston
Seigler arrived from the Milwaukee Brewers in February alongside Caleb Durbin and Andruw Monasterio. After joining the big league roster in late June, he became part of a stretch that saw Boston win at a historic pace.
He delivered a 4-for-5 performance against the Blue Jays in July that included a leadoff homer and two doubles. In August, he lined a ninth-inning triple that gave Boston the lead against the Marlins when the team needed it most.
Across 171 plate appearances this season, Seigler slashed .250/.331/.405 with three home runs and 13 RBIs. His positional versatility and switch-hitting made him a valuable bench piece for a team building toward October.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Anthony Seigler was brought back to help. Less than a week later, the Red Sox are dealing with another absence.
The wrist issue is the latest in a string of roster hits Boston has absorbed down the stretch. White is done for the regular season. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out until next week. The depth that carried this team through the summer is being tested heading into the final 10 games.
Seigler did enough during his time on the field to earn the recall. Whether he gets another chance this year depends on how far the Red Sox go in October.

Good morning! Last night, Chad Tracy gave at-bats to two pinch-hitters in the 8th inning: lefty killer Jahmai Jones and utility infielder Andruw Monasterio. Jones did his job in the 8th, singling to start the inning in place of Mickey Gasper, but would subsequently strike out to end the game in the 9th. Jones was a platoon revelation when he first arrived in Boston, but he's cooled off since then (a .200 batting average over his last 12 games), and his positional inflexibility makes him a difficult roster fit. Monasterio did not do his job last night. He struck out with the bases loaded, putting an end to the biggest threat the Sox had all night.
In light of last night's events it's time to ask: Is it time for Romy Gonzalez to get another crack? Romy theoretically combines the best of both Jones and Monasterio — he's a lefty-killer and a utility infielder. He struggled mightily in his (rushed) return to the Sox earlier this year and has recently been battling a nagging injury lately, but his AAA line reads .344/.400/.505 with 3 homers and 6 doubles. He could inject some pop just as the Sox look like they could use a little extra juice.
Use this space to talk about bench bats and whatever else you want, and, as always, be good to one another.
